title: Order types, quotes and the order book

objectives.text: Distinguish market/limit/stop and immediate-execution policies, tracing price protection, partial fills and nonexecution risk under explicit broker/venue semantics.
Compute best quotes/spread and trace a synthetic displayed-only price-time book without promoting it into a universal exchange matching rule or execution guarantee.
Fold validated level deltas into separate sides, delete zeros and sort only final active prices in side-specific order.
Maintain separate level totals and emit after every update with exact cent display and explicit missing-side markers.

blocks.markdown: A bid is buying interest, an ask/offer is selling interest. In a single synthetic book, best bid is the highest bid price and best ask the lowest ask price. For positive best quotes with bid≤ask, quoted spread=ask-bid and midpoint=(ask+bid)/2. A midpoint is a summary, not necessarily an available trade price or even an allowed tick. A crossed/locked or stale composite view needs explicit handling, not a silent assumption that arbitrage is executable. Prices, sizes, timestamps, instrument/currency and feed scope matter.

A market order seeks execution at available prices but does not guarantee the last trade, displayed quote or one average price. A buy limit permits trades at or BELOW its limit; a sell limit permits at or ABOVE. A limit controls execution price under its contract, not whether or how much fills. A marketable limit can immediately cross available opposite interest; a nonmarketable limit may rest if its instructions allow. Touching the displayed limit price is not sufficient to prove this order filled: queue position, size, eligibility and changes matter.

Order type and time-in-force are separate instructions. In the simplified IOC policy here, execute eligible quantity immediately and cancel any remainder; partial fills are allowed. FOK requires an immediate full fill or cancellation without a partial fill, subject to actual venue semantics. Day/GTC session/expiry handling and whether particular instructions are accepted vary by firm/venue. Do not assume a GTC order literally persists forever or across every session. Our code implements only snapshot buy-limit IOC, not FOK or session management.

blocks.title: A price cap does not guarantee requested quantity

steps.text: Synthetic asks are 3 shares at 1001 cents, 4 at 1002 and 5 at 1004. Incoming buy-limit IOC requests 10 shares with limit 1002.
Take 3 at 1001, leaving 7 requested. Take 4 at 1002, leaving 3. Price 1004 exceeds the buy cap, so the remainder 3 is canceled, not bought above limit and not rested.
Filled shares 7 cost 3*1001+4*1002=7011 cents before fees. Average execution price 7011/7 cents is not the limit or a simple unweighted average.

The snapshot assumes these displayed quantities remain available to this order with no hidden interest, latency, competition, fees, lot/tick restrictions or self-match controls. It is not a real fill forecast.

blocks.caption: Expected output: ([(1001, 3), (1002, 4)], 3, 7011); unchanged book [(1001, 3), (1002, 4), (1004, 5)]; then ([], 2, 0). This snapshot calculator returns hypothetical fills/canceled remainder/cost without mutating the source book. Every call is an independent scenario; repeated calls do not consume shared liquidity. Empty-side liquidity cancels all under this toy IOC policy.

blocks.markdown: In the common stock-order semantics described by SEC investor education, a stop order activates into a market order after its stop condition triggers; the trigger price is not a guaranteed execution price. A stop-limit activates into a limit order, retaining a price cap/floor but risking nonexecution. Trigger inputs may use trades or quotes and differ by broker/venue. Do not implement a generic stop trigger by comparing one arbitrary feed field or promise that a stop always bounds losses. No stop order is sent or simulated by this lesson's code.

Our teaching book contains ONLY eligible displayed ordinary limit orders for one instrument/side and distinct arrival sequence numbers. Better price has priority: higher bids or lower asks. Within the same price, earlier arrival sequence has priority. Order size does not outrank earlier arrival at the same price in this policy. The sequence is the simulator's authoritative arrival order, not a guessed ordering from client clock timestamps. This is an explicitly declared price-time toy rule, not the complete rules of Nasdaq, NSE or any other venue.

blocks.caption: Expected output: ['B', 'A', 'C']; ['E', 'D', 'F']; 1; then 2003/2. B's higher bid outranks earlier lower-priced A; at 1000 A precedes C. E's lower ask outranks D/F; at 1003 D precedes F. Best quotes 1001/1002 give spread 1 cent and midpoint 1001.5 cents, which the exact Fraction prints as 2003/2. Neither ranking nor midpoint predicts execution.

blocks.markdown: Real rulebooks can distinguish displayed/non-displayed/reserve interest, special order attributes, auctions, self-match prevention, routing and amendments that change priority. The Nasdaq order guide illustrates reserve/hidden and other attributes, so the toy's displayed-only FIFO list is intentionally incomplete. Do not copy an undated guide into a current venue adapter without verifying that market's current operative rules, protocol and test cases. Changing size/price/cancel-replace can have rule-specific priority effects; no universal amend policy is implemented here.

Aggregated price-level size does not reveal every individual queue position. A historical trade at a resting limit price does not establish that a later simulated order would have filled; existing queue, hidden size, cancellations, allocation and feed visibility can matter. Displayed depth is neither all market liquidity nor a reservation for the strategy. Before using a fill simulator, state its observable feed, priority/latency/hidden-liquidity assumptions and how those choices bias results. Later trading/research lessons implement bounded state under such contracts.

Independent transfer: reverse the sweep for a sell-limit IOC against descending bids, deriving the inequality rather than copying the buy condition. Create two same-price resting orders and show why a later larger order does not jump the earlier one in this toy FIFO. Then design a limit-touch-without-fill timeline and a stop-trigger-with-worse-execution scenario. State which rules remain unknown for a real broker/venue rather than inventing them.

References: [SEC order types/price and timing risks](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-14), [firm-specific availability](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/order-types), and [Nasdaq guide illustrating additional attributes](https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/content/ProductsServices/Trading/OrderTypesG.pdf). The guide is not used as a current operative rule adapter. All matching code implements the stated synthetic policy only.

Aggregate level quantity, not individual order identity

The public messages are level deltas (A or C, side, price, quantity). Maintain separate maps for B and S; adds accumulate and cancels subtract. Cancel validity is guaranteed: it cannot remove more than currently rests. Delete a key exactly when its total reaches zero. Side is part of the level identity, so equal numeric bid/ask prices live in different maps. This task supplies no order ids or per-order queue positions.

Final depth needs no continuous sorting

Only after the entire stream, sort bid price keys descending and ask keys ascending. Emit at most k from each, using exact integer price:quantity tokens. Unlike the neighboring spread task, these prices are printed as the supplied integer labels, not converted into two-decimal dollars. Empty side emits BIDS - or ASKS -. If fewer than k active levels exist, print them all. A zeroed price can later reappear on a fresh add.

Proof, trace and bounds

After every event, map quantity at each side/price equals the sum of all accepted deltas there, with zero entries removed. This is true initially and preserved by one signed update/deletion. Final sorting changes only presentation. Adds B 100 qty 5, B 100 qty 3, B 99 qty 7 then cancel B 99 qty 7 leave BIDS 100:8. n<=200000, k<=10, price/qty<=1e9 and totals<=2e14 fit signed 64-bit. Expected aggregation O(n), final sorting O(L log L) across L active levels, storage O(L) plus sorted keys; no O(n) scan is required after each event. Verify against a slow replay of all prior deltas and final top-k ordering, including large same-level totals and complete deletion.

blocks.source:
from collections import OrderedDict, deque
from bisect import bisect_left
import heapq
import math

def book_depth(k, messages):
    (bids, asks) = ({}, {})
    for (action, side, price, quantity) in messages:
        levels = bids if side == 'B' else asks
        levels[price] = levels.get(price, 0) + (quantity if action == 'A' else -quantity)
        if levels[price] == 0:
            del levels[price]
    lines = []
    for (label, levels, descending) in [('BIDS', bids, True), ('ASKS', asks, False)]:
        prices = sorted(levels, reverse=descending)[:k]
        content = ' '.join((f'{price}:{levels[price]}' for price in prices)) if prices else '-'
        lines.append(label + ' ' + content)
    return lines

print(*book_depth(2, [('A','B',100,5),('A','B',100,3),('A','B',99,7),('C','B',99,7),('A','S',101,4)]), sep='\n')

Observe after the event, not before

Use the same side-separated quantity fold as final-depth teaching, but this contract requires one top-of-book line after EACH event. Delete a fully canceled level before taking max(bids) and min(asks). Partial cancellations leave that price active; even an event away from the best still produces a line. Cancels are prevalidated, and the input guarantees a noncrossed book after every update.

Money display and missing values

Here prices ARE integer cents and must print as dollars with two digits: p//100 followed by p%100 zero-padded. Compute spread=ask-bid in cents first, then format it. Locked bid==ask is valid and prints 0.00 spread. If either side is empty, print - for that side and for spread; do not use 0 as an empty sentinel or invent a zero-dollar quote. A missing-side spread is undefined, not 0.00.

Trace and an honest size choice

Add bid 1000 gives 10.00 - -. Add ask 1005 gives 10.00 10.05 0.05. Add better bid 1002 gives 10.02 10.05 0.03; cancel it fully restores 10.00 10.05 0.05. With n<=3000, scanning active keys for each extrema costs O(n^2) worst-case, at most a few million key checks, with O(L) maps and O(n) returned strings. That simple implementation is appropriate for this declared task, not a low-latency engine. If the bounds or online query frequency grow, an ordered structure or carefully maintained heap needs its own stale-entry policy and proof.

from collections import OrderedDict, deque
from bisect import bisect_left
import heapq
import math

def book_spread(events):
    (bids, asks) = ({}, {})
    lines = []

    def dollars(price):
        return '-' if price is None else f'{price // 100}.{price % 100:02d}'
    for (action, side, price, quantity) in events:
        levels = bids if side == 'B' else asks
        levels[price] = levels.get(price, 0) + (quantity if action == 'A' else -quantity)
        if levels[price] == 0:
            del levels[price]
        bid = max(bids) if bids else None
        ask = min(asks) if asks else None
        spread = ask - bid if bid is not None and ask is not None else None
        lines.append(' '.join((dollars(value) for value in [bid, ask, spread])))
    return lines

print(*book_spread([('A','B',1000,3),('A','S',1005,2),('C','B',1000,3)]), sep='\n')

summary: Limit price protects a side-specific price boundary, not a full fill; stop triggers are not guaranteed prices. Quotes, midpoint and toy price-time ranking describe a declared snapshot, not a universal venue rule or a real execution promise. Practice transfer: final level depth fold. Practice transfer: every event cent spread.
